topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
summary: Discovery call to understand Pegasus Systems' latency/throughput requirements for a real-time chat/assist product. Customer is evaluating Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment models. Key requirements: p95 under 350ms for short-turn prompts, 1000 concurrent streams at peak, streaming partials, and acceptable token/sec throughput for longer context batches. Next steps: send benchmarks, schedule perf run, share security docs.
transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-12-15 14:30 UTC | Duration: 48 minutes | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Pegasus VP Eng), Sofia Alvarez (ML Eng), Daniel Park (Infra)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, um uh today we wanted to, uh, just run through your latency and throughput needs and see where Redwood fits. Marcus, do you want to kick off with a quick overview of the product and the SLA needs?
[00:15] Marcus Lee: Sure yeah, thanks Alex. We're building a customer-facing assistant, real time chat and some contextual retrieval. Our p95 target for short prompts is around 300 to 350 milliseconds including network, we usually budget ~50-100ms for network. We also have longer flows that stream tokens back, so streaming latency and partials are important.
[00:35] Priya Nair: Got it. When you say streaming, is that token-by-token low-latency streaming or chunked partials?
[00:45] Sofia Alvarez: Token-by-token ideally, because we show progressive UI to the user. The UX drops a lot if partials are delayed.
[00:55] Alex Chen: Okay. And concurrency — what concurrency numbers are we talking about?
[01:03] Marcus Lee: Peak concurrency around 1000 concurrent sessions, average maybe 200-300. Typical prompt length is 30-80 tokens for quick queries, but occasionally 1k-2k tokens for longer contexts.
[01:20] Daniel Park: And from infra perspective we need predictable tail latency. We're also very sensitive to cost; if Dedicated is much cheaper per token for our workload we'll consider it but we need the isolation for some enterprise customers.
[01:36] Priya Nair: Makes sense — we typically see Hosted for fast time-to-value, Dedicated for predictable throughput and cost smoothing, and Private for VPC/on-prem for highest control. For p95 under 350ms for short prompts, we need to look at model selection, batching strategy, and whether KV cache is effective for your prompt patterns.
[01:58] Marcus Lee: Can you give an example of what model and hardware mix would hit 300ms p95?
[02:06] Priya Nair: Roughly speaking, for short 30-80 token prompts we hit sub-300ms p95 on optimized Llama-3 variants on A100-class or newer GPUs with proper batching and no heavy quantization. On Hopper/RTX-class with quantization it varies. Also streaming adds a small overhead because of the early token flushes.
[02:28] Marcus Lee: Are you mentioning A100 — we run mostly on GCP and AWS, what are availability and regions like for Dedicated?
[02:36] Alex Chen: We have Dedicated pools in major regions, we can provision GCP/AWS with A100 or H100 depending on contract. For Private we can support customer-provided infra but that'll require ops setup.
[02:49] Sofia Alvarez: How do you measure token/sec and concurrency in your benchmarks? We need a reproducible metric because our load is bursty.
[02:58] Priya Nair: We provide a benchmark spreadsheet — token/sec is measured as tokens generated per second under sustained load with configured concurrency. We also include p95/p99 latencies and token cost. For streaming workloads we report first-byte latency and time-to-last-token.
[03:16] Marcus Lee: Can you run a sample with our payloads and show p95 including network?
[03:21] Alex Chen: Yes, that's part of the perf run. Ideally you send sample payloads and we run hosted and Dedicated variants so you can compare token/sec and cost per 1M tokens.
[03:33] Daniel Park: What about KMS and encryption? For some of our customers we need HSM-backed keys and key rotation audits.
[03:41] Alex Chen: We support KMS integrations and HSM for Private deployments, and our audit logs integrate with your SIEM. We'll share the SOC 2 and security pack after the call.
[03:53] Sofia Alvarez: Any gotchas with KV cache — we use repeated user context a lot, would that dramatically reduce latency?
[04:00] Priya Nair: Yes, if you have repeat prefixes we can cache KV state to avoid recomputing attention for previous tokens. In practice that can reduce token compute by 40-60% for repeated flows. Note sometimes transcription shows K V cache as two words in logs, but it's the KV cache.
[04:20] Marcus Lee: For the 1000 concurrent sessions, how does Redwood handle batching vs streaming? We're worried that batching to improve throughput will hurt p95 for streaming sessions.
[04:32] Priya Nair: That's the tradeoff — continuous batching helps cost but increases queuing. We have workload-aware batching where we route low-latency streaming requests to a lower-batch fast lane and batch non-streaming requests more aggressively. You can also reserve Dedicated capacity to guarantee concurrency.
[04:52] Alex Chen: Another option is hybrid routing — route premium customers to Dedicated low-latency pool and others to Hosted or burst capacity. That keeps p95 predictable for critical flows.
[05:05] Marcus Lee: Okay. What about quantization and quality? Our evaluation is strict; we can't degrade answer quality.
[05:13] Priya Nair: We recommend model/quantization combos per workload. For high-quality latency-sensitive flows we suggest lighter quantization Q4_0 on Llama variants; heavy int8 can sometimes affect quality. We'll provide model-based benchmarks tied to your eval prompts.
[05:31] Sofia Alvarez: Do you support function calling and structured outputs? We use tool-calls to fetch data mid-conversation.
[05:37] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood supports function/tool calling and structured output. Tool calls sometimes add an extra hop but we can pipeline them to reduce impact.
[05:45] [00:06:00] Priya Nair: Quick sidebar — what's your timeline for POC and rollout?
[06:03] Marcus Lee: We'd like a POC in Jan, ideally a 2-week perf validation first half of Jan, then pilot in Feb, prod in Q2. Need to align procurement and security review.
[06:15] Daniel Park: Procurement will require SOC2, SAML/SSO integration, RBAC, and contract language around data retention and deletion.
[06:24] Alex Chen: Understood. We'll loop in our security team and SEs. We'll also share a proposed canary deployment plan for rollouts.
[06:32] Sofia Alvarez: For the perf run, can you measure p95 with and without KV cache and with streaming turned on?
[06:39] Priya Nair: Yes — typical matrix: model variant x quantization x KV cache on/off x streaming vs non-streaming x concurrency levels. We'll run representative loads at 100, 300, 600, and 1000 concurrent sessions.
[06:57] Marcus Lee: On cost, can you ballpark what Dedicated might save us per token at our scale?
[07:04] Alex Chen: Ballpark depends a lot on model and utilization. If you reach sustained high utilization, Dedicated can be 20-40% cheaper per token compared to Hosted because of reserved capacity and optimized batching. We'll include cost-per-1M token scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[07:20] Daniel Park: Any notes about regional fallbacks? We need cross-region failover for low-latency users in EU and NA.
[07:28] Priya Nair: Yes, we have smart routing by region and automated fallback to compatible model variants in other regions if capacity is constrained; we can keep user affinity to minimize cold-starts.
[07:40] Marcus Lee: Are there limits on streaming token/sec per connection? We've seen rate limiting at providers that kills UX on bursty typing.
[07:48] Alex Chen: We expose per-connection rate limits and allow you to configure streaming flush sizes. We also support client-side pacing and server-side shaping. For bursty typing you can use local debouncing to aggregate keystrokes — but we'll test with your real UX traces.
[08:07] Sofia Alvarez: Regarding benchmarks, do you report first-byte p95 as well as final-token p95? For streaming the first-byte matters a lot.
[08:15] Priya Nair: Yes, we report first-byte, median and p95 for both first-byte and time-to-last-token.
[08:22] Marcus Lee: What's the instrumentation? We need traces we can ingest into our observability stack.
[08:28] Alex Chen: We provide tracing hooks, per-route dashboards, and token-level cost/latency breakdowns. We can push traces to your tracing backend or provide logs.
[08:38] [00:09:00] Daniel Park: Anything else on compliance? We have some healthcare customers so data residency might be required.
[08:44] Priya Nair: For regulated workloads we'd suggest Private VPC or on-prem; that supports KMS/HSM and local data residency. For Hosted we can provide region guarantees and data retention configs but Private is the path for strict residency.
[08:58] Marcus Lee: Ok that makes sense. For the POC, who will run the perf tests and what do you need from us?
[09:05] Priya Nair: We'll lead the perf test with your infra team. We need sample payloads, expected user concurrency curves, and a list of eval prompts for quality validation. We'll also need access to a test account and temporary SSO credentials.
[09:18] Marcus Lee: I'll get those to you by Wednesday.
[09:22] Alex Chen: Great. We'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and security pack today. Priya will follow up with the perf plan and schedule.
[09:29] Sofia Alvarez: One last question — do you do token-level caching or prefix caching?
[09:35] Priya Nair: We do prefix/KV caching which essentially caches the KV state for repeated prefixes — it's not token-level caching in the sense of full output caching, but it reduces compute on repeated context.
[09:47] Marcus Lee: Awesome. Thanks everyone.
[09:50] Alex Chen: Thanks Marcus, Sofia, Daniel — we'll follow up with next steps.

Recap: 1) Redwood to send benchmark spreadsheet and SOC2/security pack 2) Priya to draft perf plan and run hosted + Dedicated perf runs with Pegasus payloads 3) Marcus to provide payloads, concurrency profiles, and p95 targets

Links referenced: Benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat), Security pack (link to internal redwood security docs), Perf-run template (short note)

Customer prioritized streaming first-byte p95 and 1000 concurrent sessions
